name: ACC1b-6-a-credential-shadow-ships-to-the-client
note: The whole row includes secret_hash. A hash is a credential's shadow and there is no reason to ship one.

name: ACC1b-7-an-unusable-guest-name-is-minted-anyway
old: if (!nameIsIssuable(name) || !isGuestShaped(name)) throw new Error(`guestName produced an unusable name: ${name}`);
new: if (false) throw new Error(`guestName produced an unusable name: ${name}`);
why: The banks are the game's own and every name they can produce is issuable - a pin derives the bank's whole alphabet and proves it. So removing the check changes no outcome today. It is kept because a name that cannot ride a token is an account that cannot play, and the place to learn that is the mint rather than the player's first connection.

name: ACC1b-8-a-short-secret-is-looked-up-anyway
old: if (typeof secret !== 'string' || secret.length < 16 || secret.length > 128) return null;
why: A wrong secret of any length hashes to something no row holds, so the lookup answers null either way. The bound is here to say no before a digest and a query rather than after them, which is the same reason the Worker bounds a body before parsing it.

name: ACC1b-9-the-guest-shape-enumerates-an-alphabet-again
old: export const GUEST_NAME_RE = /^\S+ \S+$/;

The law is unchanged; only the address is. test/mutantdrift.test.js caught the move.

name: ACC1b-16-the-generator-hands-out-a-name-the-wire-cannot-carry
note: AUDIT-ACC F7 put back: the single unfiltered draw. Four of the bank's 173,330 names are 25 characters against a NAME_MAX of 24, so createGuest threw and /v1/auth/guest answered 500 for about one guest in 43,000. It survived ACC1b's own testing because that pin sampled draws - eighteen of them - and four in 173,330 is invisible to a sample. The pin that kills this enumerates the whole space and then drives the exact draw.

name: ACC1b-22-the-credential-goes-back-in-the-url
old: const secret = bearer ?? (request.method === 'POST' ? body.secret : null);
note: AUDIT-ACC F13 put back verbatim. A URL is written into Cloudflare's request logs, into any Referer the page emits, and into browser history - so this puts the session secret in all three. It reads harmless because the route is read-only, which is the excuse that let it ship.

name: ACC1b-23-the-body-overrides-the-header
old: const secret = bearer ?? (request.method === 'POST' ? body.secret : null);
note: Two sources for one credential need a stated winner, or a caller that sends both gets whichever the implementation happened to prefer - and that answer changes the day somebody reorders the expression.

name: ACC1b-24-the-preflight-forbids-the-header
old: 'access-control-allow-headers': 'content-type, authorization',
note: The header the credential now rides in is one no browser will send unless the preflight allows it. Every cross-origin authenticated call would fail, and the failure would look like a CORS problem rather than the missing word it is.
